title: Cultural identity and behavioral participation: The role of Hakka landscapes in campus heritage education—A case study of a middle school in changting county
content:
by Jing Luo, Lan Yang, De-zheng Kong

In the era of globalization, cultural landscapes are becoming increasingly vital for the transmission of cultural heritage. This study aims to investigate how campus landscapes embedded with cultural symbols are associated with students’ cultural identity and behavioral participation. We conducted an empirical study of 516 middle school students in Changting County using stratified convenience sampling and structural equation modeling (SEM). The research tests a conceptual model that progresses from Hakka cultural landscape perception, through cultural experience and identity, to cultural behavioral participation. The results reveal that: (1) Hakka cultural landscape perception shows a dual-pathway pattern, with symbolic recognition perception and cultural meaning perception both significantly predicting cultural experience (β = 0.358,0.272); (2) the chain mediation model of perception-experience-identity-behavior is supported by the data, with cultural experience and cultural identity serving as key mediators; (3) cultural identity demonstrates the strongest predictive association with behaviors (online behavior β = 0.543, offline behavior β = 0.343); (4) symbolic recognition perception and cultural meaning perception show differentiated associations with online and offline participation. This study enriches the application of Place Identity Theory and Cultural Identity Theory in educational contexts, providing empirical guidance for campus cultural landscape design, and offers a theoretical reference for future research on the contextualized transmission of regional ethnic cultures.
author: Jing Luo
